Attachments R&D daily sprint 
Meeting records Transcript 
Summary
Amir Houieh provided updates on website development, confirming work completion and readiness for deployment, and also shared an updated TSV file with new session tracking metrics for Cibil with Noémi Biró. Participants discussed the need for immediate preparation for planning the entire month of March with Melissa, who has signed the contract, and addressed a major concern regarding potential architectural changes to Cibil if Melissa expresses uncertainty about the chat functionality. Amir Houieh and Noémi Biró agreed to an internal brainstorming session later today to explore the implications of potentially removing the chat feature from Cibil entirely.
Details
Personal Wellness and Scheduling Updates: Noémi Biró mentioned they have not been sleeping well, which their smart ring indicates, possibly due to a combination of their workouts and lack of sleep. Amir Houieh needed to leave the meeting at 12:00 PM for a dentist appointment and noted that Gabber was running 15 minutes late (00:00:00). They decided to conduct a quick update now and potentially catch up later (00:02:26).
Website Development Status: Amir Houieh reported they completed their planned website work, and if Noémi Biró wants to work on it, they can clone the main branch and make adjustments on a new branch using tools like Cursor (00:00:00). Amir Houieh confirmed they sent the repository link after Noémi Biró requested it. They also worked on the Google search engine metadata, including images, so that the website is ready for deployment (00:07:33).
Upcoming Planning with Melissa: Melissa has signed the contract, and Amir Houieh sent an email to establish a start date. They agreed that they need to be prepared by tomorrow to plan the whole month of March, including the topics they want to focus on (00:02:26).
Implications of Potential Chat Changes in Cibil: The memory consistency of Cibil is a known issue, with some users reporting that Cibil forgets the current date or month. The main concern, however, stems from Melissa expressing uncertainty about the chat functionality, which would represent a fundamental change to the architecture and increase the workload beyond what was initially accommodated. They agreed this situation needs to be communicated transparently with Melissa (00:03:38).
Internal Brainstorming Session for Cibil Architecture: Amir Houieh suggested a brainstorming session among the three participants to explore the implications of removing the chat feature entirely, which would likely create more design tasks than development work. Noémi Biró suggested setting aside an hour after tomorrow's daily check-in for an internal update on Cibil (00:04:44). They agreed to schedule a meeting for later today at 5:00 PM, or earlier if possible, to discuss this further (00:05:50).
Website Repository and Tools: Noémi Biró confirmed they have the Cursor application and asked Amir Houieh to send the repository link, which they promptly did (00:07:33). Amir Houieh is available after 1:30 PM following their dentist appointment if anything else comes up .
App Duration Metrics Update: Amir Houieh provided Noémi Biró with an updated TSV file that includes three new columns for session tracking within Cibil. The new columns track the average duration, the longest duration, and the total time a user spent. Since Cibil lacks a natural session concept, a session is defined by a one-hour gap in user inactivity (00:07:33).
Suggested next steps
Noémi Biró will clone the main branch, make adjustments to the website using cursor or cloud, and create a new branch.
Amir Houieh will send the repository to Noémi Biró.
The group will have an internal check-in, possibly today at 5 PM, to discuss Cibil and the implications of stopping the chat feature.

📝 Notes
Feb 26, 2026
R&D daily sprint
Invited Amir Houieh Unbody io Noémi Biró Gabor Kerekes
Attachments R&D daily sprint 
Meeting records Transcript 
Summary
The meeting centered on the Mycelium system, described as the "invisible kernel" or back end for a personal OS that ingests a user's digital production to surface insights and organize information via emergent themes and generative UI capabilities. The discussion, featuring a demonstration by Gabor Kerekes, clarified that the displayed interface was a bookmarking app, one front end for the system, and emphasized the need for a ubiquitous, OS-level presence for Mycelium, with careful attention to data capture and privacy using technologies like ScreenPipe. Gabor Kerekes will create a repository for the hardcoded source code to allow others to build a use case on top of Nexus, recognizing the prototype's aesthetic and semantic analysis capabilities as a strong test scenario for the Nexus framework.
Details
Mycelium as a Centralized System: The mycelium system is described as a substrate that contains a representation of a user's interests and priorities, serving as a back end or the "invisible kernel" of a personal operating system. It ingests various forms of digital production, such as conversations, chat logs, bookmarks, and notes, and then surfaces insights (00:00:00) (00:05:02). The system operates in the cloud or on the user's machine, processing data in the background (00:05:02).
The Bookmarking Interface and Data Ingestion: The discussion clarifies that the displayed item is one interface to the mycelium—specifically, the bookmarking app—and not the mycelium itself, which is the back end (00:02:58) (00:05:02). The proposed data capture mechanism for bookmarking would be a native Mac OS widget, which can be triggered with a shortcut to take a screenshot of what the user is seeing, allowing capture outside of a browser (00:04:05).
Intelligent Data Retrieval and Semantic Analysis: The bookmarking interface is designed to retrieve and process bookmarks intelligently, going beyond a simple database with semantic search (00:06:06). Gabor Kerekes demonstrated that the system is expected to digest data and surface insights, such as identifying patterns like a user's "hoarding mode" or the contradiction between massive ingestion and rare reflection (00:08:07). The system's observations, like linking a user's saving habits to a quote found in their notes, are valued as a "mirror" to the user's life (00:09:43).
Organization and Thematic Digestion: The system organizes bookmarks by identifying emergent themes, which are produced by cross-referencing bookmarks with conversations and journaling data to summarize what is "at the top of [the] mind". When a theme, or "thread," is selected, the interface displays related notes, articles, conversations, tools, and tensions relevant to that topic, such as "building a cognitive exoskeleton" (00:11:21). The system offers a chat input for querying the data, allowing users to ask for specific information or connections between disparate topics (00:13:10).
Adaptive and Generative User Interface (UI): The design vision includes a generative UI where users can communicate with the interface to request different viewing formats, such as asking it to organize a list of bookmarks as a mind map (00:11:21) (00:16:01). The concept involves the Nexus system and agents observing how users interact with the application to learn their preferences, such as defaulting to a mind map view for a specific topic if that is the user's usual choice (00:17:17). The preference for either a visual canvas or a simple list depends on the user and the topic, underscoring the need for personalization (00:19:50).
Mycelium as a Ubiquitous Personal Operating System: The system is envisioned to be embedded everywhere, such as within Google Calendar or during email composition, functioning as a "fourth person" in a conversation by listening and providing real-time, relevant context (00:21:09) (00:23:29). This approach aims for the system to live at the OS level, integrating with existing applications and having the ability to see the user's screen to know what they are doing (00:24:31). Screen-capture technologies like ScreenPipe, which uses local AI for privacy-respecting data capture, were noted as a potential component to log user activity and generate memory (00:26:04).
Data Capture and Privacy Considerations: Discussions covered the need for careful management of digital footprints, distinguishing between observed online activities and connected integrations like Google Drive. For user privacy, the proposed system should allow filtering or white-listing of content that is always observed, and users should be able to explicitly enable observation for other activities only when needed, such as when using a specific application like the terminal (00:27:04). The system should ideally be a native tool within the operating system, with context-sensitive utilities that change based on what the user is interacting with, such as an image or a text area (00:29:46).
Nexus Use Case and Development Focus: The aesthetic and semantic analysis capabilities shown by the prototype are considered a strong test scenario for the Nexus framework (00:18:45). It was identified that an interesting use case for the learners in Nexus would be capturing interaction patterns with the generative UI, such as always requesting a mind map for a specific topic (00:31:07). Gabor Kerekes will create a repository for the hardcoded source code to allow others to build a use case on top of Nexus (00:35:48).
Prototype Development Tools: The current prototype and conceptual clarifications were developed using Claude for brainstorming and distilling first principles, while Gemini 3.1 Pro was used for the actual building of the code (00:37:14). The prototype is viewed as a good proof of concept because the insights were generated from real data by the same AI that is intended to live inside the app (00:35:48).
Suggested next steps
Gabor Kerekes will refine the prototype to show the larger vision and a more complete picture of the mycelium system.
Gabor Kerekes will make a repo for the source code of the hardcoded mycelium prototype and send it to Amir Houieh.
